questions.stem: A 71 year old man has a 6 week history of an ulcer on his right heel that keeps him awake at night. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and has hypertension. The ulcer is 1.5 cm, deep, with sharply defined edges and a dry, pale base that does not bleed when cleaned. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A deep, punched-out, dry, pale heel ulcer that hurts at night in a smoker is arterial; a venous ulcer is shallow, irregular and exudative over the medial gaiter area.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: dry, pale base that does not bleed
steps.x: Distal site, rest pain, vascular risk factors and a punched-out dry base.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial ulcer.

elim: Painless, over pressure points such as metatarsal heads, with lost sensation.
Heel is a pressure site, but he is mobile and the ulcer is painful at rest with risk factors for PAD.
Rapidly enlarging ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge, linked to IBD.
Shallow, irregular, moist ulcer above the medial malleolus with pigmentation.

steps.x: **A. Arterial ulcer.** Punched out + dry + painful at rest + smoker = arterial ulcer.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a painful, deep ulcer over her left lateral malleolus. She has type 2 diabetes and a 35 pack-year smoking history. The ulcer edges are well defined and the base is dry. The surrounding skin is pale and the foot is cool to touch. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the left leg?
o: Haemosiderin staining of the gaiter area
questions.e: Arterial ulcers come with a cold limb and reduced or absent pulses because of peripheral arterial disease; the other options are signs of chronic venous disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
This is an arterial ulcer: the limb is cold with reduced pulses.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Absent dorsalis pedis pulse.

elim: A venous sign from extravasated red cells.
Woody induration from chronic venous hypertension.
Points to venous disease or heart failure, not arterial insufficiency.
Varicose veins go with venous ulcers.

steps.x: **A. Absent dorsalis pedis pulse.** Arterial ulcer = cold limb, weak or absent pulses, low ABPI.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with peripheral arterial disease is seen in the vascular clinic with a 1 cm ulcer on the tip of his left third toe. He has smoked for 50 years. The ulcer is deep with well-defined edges. The left foot is cool and pale with no palpable pedal pulses. His BP is 158/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely appearance of the ulcer base?
o: Dry, pale base with minimal bleeding
Friable base with an everted, rolled edge
Moist granulation tissue with heavy exudate
Necrotic base with a violaceous undermined edge
Slough over a base that bleeds easily on contact
questions.e: An arterial ulcer has a dry, pale wound bed that bleeds little because there is little blood supply; heavy exudate and granulation are typical of venous ulcers.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: tip of his left third toe
steps.x: Toe-tip ulcer in a pulseless foot is arterial, so the base is poorly perfused.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dry, pale base with minimal bleeding.

elim: Suggests malignancy such as squamous cell carcinoma.
Classic venous ulcer base.
Pyoderma gangrenosum.
A well-perfused wound bleeds easily; ischaemic tissue does not.

steps.x: **A. Dry, pale base with minimal bleeding.** Arterial = dry, pale, little bleeding. Venous = moist, exudative, granulating.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has intermittent claudication of the right calf at 100 metres. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has hypercholesterolaemia. His right ABPI is 0.6. He is worried because his father had a leg ulcer from 'poor circulation'. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site for an arterial ulcer to develop?
o: Gaiter area above the medial malleolus
Plantar surface of the first metatarsal head
questions.e: Arterial ulcers form at distal, poorly perfused sites: toes, heel and lateral malleolus.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
He has PAD; ulcers form where perfusion is worst, distally.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tips of the toes.

elim: The classic site of venous ulcers.
Typical neuropathic (diabetic) ulcer site under pressure.
Proximal and well perfused; not an ulcer site.
A pressure ulcer site in immobile patients.

steps.x: **E. Tips of the toes.** Arterial ulcers: toes, heel, lateral malleolus.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a punched-out, painful ulcer on his left fifth toe. He drinks 12 units of alcohol a week, has a BMI of 27 kg/m² and smokes 30 cigarettes a day. He had a DVT 10 years ago. His ankle-brachial pressure index is 0.55 on the left. His BP is 144/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for his ulcer?
questions.e: Smoking is the strongest modifiable driver of peripheral arterial disease and arterial ulcers; previous DVT is a risk factor for venous ulcers.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Arterial ulcer from PAD; the PAD drivers are smoking, diabetes, lipids and hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Smoking.

elim: 12 units a week is within limits and not a key PAD driver.
Non-modifiable and a weaker association than smoking.
A mild contributor, far weaker than heavy smoking.
Causes venous hypertension and venous ulcers, not arterial ulcers.

steps.x: **E. Smoking.** Smoking is the key PAD risk factor to tackle.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has a deep, painful ulcer on her right heel and calf pain when she walks uphill. She has never smoked. Her past history includes asthma, hypothyroidism, osteoarthritis, gout and a condition for which she takes metformin and gliclazide. The right foot is cool with weak pulses. Her BP is 136/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which condition in her history most increases her risk of this ulcer?
questions.e: Diabetes (metformin and gliclazide) accelerates atherosclerosis and is a major risk factor for PAD and arterial ulcers.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: calf pain when she walks uphill
steps.x: Claudication and weak pulses mean PAD; her PAD driver here is diabetes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

elim: Not a risk factor for arterial disease.
Causes joint inflammation, not limb ischaemia.
Can raise lipids slightly but is not the main driver here.
May limit walking but does not narrow arteries.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.** PAD risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has a deep ulcer on his left lateral malleolus with well-defined edges. He has angina and smokes. The left foot is cold with no palpable pulses and his left ABPI is 0.5. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which feature of the history is he most likely to report?
o: Aching that is relieved by raising the leg
Heaviness of the legs at the end of the day
Itching of the skin around the ulcer
Pain at night eased by hanging the leg out of bed
questions.e: Arterial ulcers are severely painful, classically even at rest, and pain is relieved by dependency because gravity helps perfusion.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Arterial ulcer with a low ABPI: expect rest pain relieved by dependency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pain at night eased by hanging the leg out of bed.

elim: Venous: elevation helps drainage but worsens arterial pain.
A symptom of venous insufficiency.
Venous eczema.
Neuropathic ulcers are painless; arterial ulcers are very painful.

steps.x: **E. Pain at night eased by hanging the leg out of bed.** Arterial ulcer pain is worse lying flat and eased by dangling the leg.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has a small painful ulcer on her right big toe. She has hypertension and hyperlipidaemia and smoked for 40 years. The right foot is pale with a weak dorsalis pedis pulse. Her right ABPI is 0.7. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 156/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which symptom is she most likely to describe?
o: Back pain radiating down the leg when standing
Burning pain in both soles at night
Calf pain on walking that settles within minutes of rest
Morning stiffness of the ankle lasting an hour
Sudden onset of a cold, numb leg 2 hours ago
questions.e: Arterial ulcers occur with intermittent calf claudication from PAD: reproducible calf pain on exertion relieved by rest.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: painful ulcer on her right big toe
steps.x: PAD with an ABPI below 0.8 gives intermittent claudication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Calf pain on walking that settles within minutes of rest.

elim: Spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication) is eased by sitting or bending.
Peripheral neuropathy.
Inflammatory arthritis.
Acute limb ischaemia, an emergency, not a chronic ulcer.

steps.x: **C. Calf pain on walking that settles within minutes of rest.** Arterial ulcer + calf claudication = chronic PAD.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a painful ulcer on his left heel. He smokes and has type 2 diabetes. His left ABPI is 0.55. He mentions that he no longer needs to shave his shins. His temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 148/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on inspection of the left lower leg?
o: Brown pigmentation above the medial malleolus
Thickened, woody induration of the calf
questions.e: Chronic ischaemia causes atrophic skin: hair loss and thin, shiny skin. The other options are signs of chronic venous disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: painful ulcer on his left heel
no longer needs to shave his shins
steps.x: Chronic arterial insufficiency starves skin appendages: hair falls out, skin thins.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hairless, thin, shiny skin.

elim: White scarred patches of chronic venous disease.
Haemosiderin staining in venous disease.
Lipodermatosclerosis, a venous change.
Venous hypertension, not ischaemia.

steps.x: **C. Hairless, thin, shiny skin.** Arterial skin: hairless, thin, shiny, pale. Venous skin: brown, hard, eczematous.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has had a painful arterial ulcer on the tip of his right second toe for 4 months. He still smokes. Over the last 10 days the whole toe has turned black, cold and numb, and the skin is shrivelled and dry. There is no discharge or spreading redness. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 80 bpm.
questions.q: Which complication has developed?
questions.e: Untreated arterial ulcers progress to gangrene, then critical limb ischaemia and amputation; a black, cold, shrivelled toe is dead tissue.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Black, dry, numb tissue distal to an arterial ulcer is gangrene.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gangrene.

elim: Hot, red, swollen spreading skin, not black and cold.
Squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic scar or ulcer over years, not a black toe.
Bone infection: probe to bone, fever, raised inflammatory markers.
Itchy scaly skin in venous disease.

steps.x: **B. Gangrene.** Arterial ulcer course: gangrene, then critical limb ischaemia, then amputation.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has a non-healing ulcer on her left heel and has been sleeping in a chair for 3 weeks because of foot pain at night. She smokes and has hypertension. The left foot is pale and cold with no palpable pulses. Investigations: left ABPI 0.38. Her temperature is 36.9°C and BP 160/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rest pain for more than 2 weeks with tissue loss and an ABPI below 0.5 is critical limb ischaemia; acute limb ischaemia develops over hours.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: sleeping in a chair for 3 weeks
steps.x: Rest pain, tissue loss and a very low ABPI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Critical limb ischaemia.

elim: Sudden onset over hours with the 6 Ps, not 3 weeks of rest pain.
A warm, swollen calf with normal pulses.
Pain only on exertion; she has rest pain and tissue loss.
Neurogenic leg pain with normal pulses.

steps.x: **B. Critical limb ischaemia.** ABPI under 0.5 + rest pain + ulcer = critical limb ischaemia: refer urgently.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with an arterial ulcer on his right fourth toe is examined on the couch. When his legs are raised to 45 degrees the right foot turns white within a minute. He then sits up and hangs both legs over the side of the couch. His right ABPI is 0.45. His BP is 150/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely appearance of the right foot after hanging it down?
o: Blue and swollen with pitting oedema
questions.e: Dependent rubor: the dependent ischaemic foot goes dusky red as maximally dilated, poorly functioning vessels fill with blood (positive Buerger's test).

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: hangs both legs over the side
steps.x: Pallor on elevation, then dependent rubor: Buerger's test positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Red and dusky.

elim: Suggests venous obstruction or DVT.
Lipodermatosclerosis of venous disease.
Normal response; his foot is ischaemic.
That is the colour on elevation, not on dependency.

steps.x: **D. Red and dusky.** Elevation = pallor, dependency = dusky red (dependent rubor).

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a painful 1 cm ulcer on the tip of his left big toe. Sensation to a 10 g monofilament and vibration is normal in both feet. The left foot is cool with absent pedal pulses. Investigations: left ABPI 0.6. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A painful toe-tip ulcer with intact sensation, absent pulses and an ABPI below 0.8 is arterial; a neuropathic ulcer is painless with lost sensation.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: Sensation to a 10 g monofilament and vibration is normal
steps.x: Diabetes alone does not mean neuropathic: here sensation is intact and the pulses are absent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial ulcer.

elim: Painless, at pressure points, with lost monofilament sensation.
Over bony prominences in immobile patients.
Raised everted edge in a long-standing wound.
Gaiter area, with normal pulses.

steps.x: **A. Arterial ulcer.** Painful + intact sensation + low ABPI = arterial, even in a diabetic.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has a punched-out ulcer over her right lateral malleolus that has not healed for 2 months. She has hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and a 45 pack-year smoking history. The foot is cold with absent pulses and her right ABPI is 0.58. Her temperature is 36.6°C and BP 162/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of the ulcer?
questions.e: Arterial ulcers result from tissue ischaemia due to reduced arterial supply, usually atherosclerotic PAD.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Low ABPI and absent pulses: arterial supply is reduced.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Peripheral arterial disease.

elim: Causes venous ulcers in the gaiter area with normal pulses.
Causes painless neuropathic ulcers.
Pressure ulcers in immobile people.
Purpuric, multiple ulcers with systemic features.

steps.x: **B. Peripheral arterial disease.** Arterial ulcer = ischaemia from PAD.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man is referred with a leg ulcer. He smokes and has angina. A photograph shows a round 1 cm ulcer over the left lateral malleolus with a sharp edge, as if cut with a punch, and a dry pale base. His left foot is cool and there is little bleeding when the ulcer is cleaned. His BP is 150/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly suggests an arterial rather than a venous cause?
o: Sharp punched-out edge with a dry base
questions.e: The signature arterial ulcer is well defined and punched out with a dry bed and minimal bleeding, unlike the irregular, exudative venous ulcer.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: sharp edge, as if cut with a punch
steps.x: The ulcer itself tells you most: punched out and dry.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sharp punched-out edge with a dry base.

elim: Both types occur on the lower leg; the malleolus side matters more.
Does not separate arterial from venous ulcers.
Supports vascular disease but is not a feature of the ulcer.
Size does not distinguish the two.

steps.x: **D. Sharp punched-out edge with a dry base.** Punched out + dry = arterial; irregular + wet = venous.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman sees her GP with a painful ulcer on her right heel for 5 weeks. She smokes and has type 2 diabetes. The ulcer is deep and dry with defined edges. The right foot is cool and the posterior tibial pulse is faint. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 146/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: ABPI is the first-line bedside test for arterial insufficiency; below 0.8 indicates significant arterial disease.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: painful ulcer on her right heel
deep and dry with defined edges
steps.x: Suspected arterial ulcer: quantify the arterial supply first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ankle-brachial pressure index.

elim: Gold standard to map disease before revascularisation, not the first test.
Assesses venous reflux for venous ulcers.
Looks for osteomyelitis or gas, not arterial disease.
Only if there are signs of infection.

steps.x: **A. Ankle-brachial pressure index.** Arterial ulcer: palpate pulses, then ABPI first.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man is seen in clinic with a painful, punched-out ulcer on his left fifth toe. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and has hypertension. The ulcer base is dry. A medical student is asked to examine the leg before any tests are booked. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 150/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step in examining the left leg?
o: Test sensation with a 10 g monofilament
questions.e: The first-line assessment of a suspected arterial ulcer is to palpate the peripheral pulses, then measure the ABPI.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Suspected arterial ulcer: check the arterial supply at the bedside.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palpate the peripheral pulses.

elim: Used when DVT is suspected.
Checks for osteomyelitis in infected ulcers.
Assesses venous valve competence in varicose veins.
For neuropathic ulcers; useful later but not the key first step.

steps.x: **B. Palpate the peripheral pulses.** First-line: palpate pulses, then ABPI.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has a painful ulcer on her right lateral malleolus. She smokes and has hyperlipidaemia. Her right ankle systolic pressure is 104 mmHg and her brachial systolic pressure is 145 mmHg. Her temperature is 36.5°C and pulse rate 76 bpm.

visual.title: Right ABPI
visual.caption: An ABPI below 0.8 is diagnostic of significant arterial disease.

questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of her result?
o: Falsely raised value from calcified arteries
questions.e: ABPI = 104/145 = 0.72; an ABPI below 0.8 is diagnostic of significant arterial disease, while below 0.5 suggests critical limb ischaemia.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Work out the ABPI: 104 divided by 145 is about 0.72.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Significant peripheral arterial disease.

elim: Suggested by an ABPI below 0.5.
Gives an ABPI above 1.3.
Normal is 0.8 or above in these notes (usually 0.9 to 1.3).
ABPI measures arterial supply, not venous reflux.

steps.x: **D. Significant peripheral arterial disease.** ABPI under 0.8 = significant arterial disease.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has a deep ulcer on his left heel and pain in the foot at night. He has smoked for 55 years. The foot is cold and pale with no palpable pulses. Investigations: left ankle systolic pressure 58 mmHg, left brachial systolic pressure 148 mmHg. His BP is 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of his ankle-brachial pressure index?
questions.e: ABPI = 58/148 = 0.39; a severely reduced ABPI below 0.5 suggests critical limb ischaemia, matching his rest pain and tissue loss.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: pain in the foot at night
steps.x: Calculate: 58 divided by 148 is about 0.39.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Critical limb ischaemia.

elim: Mild disease gives an ABPI near 0.8, not 0.39.
Normal is 0.8 or above.
Calcification falsely raises the ABPI above 1.3.
Not measured by ABPI.

steps.x: **A. Critical limb ischaemia.** ABPI under 0.5 = critical limb ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a non-healing arterial ulcer on her right big toe despite stopping smoking and taking clopidogrel and atorvastatin. She has rest pain. Her right ABPI is 0.44. The vascular team plan revascularisation and need to know where the arteries are blocked. Her eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Ankle-brachial pressure index repeated after exercise
questions.e: CT angiography is the gold standard, mapping the location and extent of arterial blockage before angioplasty or bypass.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: need to know where the arteries are blocked
steps.x: Before intervention you need an anatomical map of the arteries.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CT angiography.

elim: Quantifies severity but does not show where the blockage is.
Used for suspected venous thromboembolism.
Looks at veins, not arteries.
Shows bone and gas, not arterial anatomy.

steps.x: **B. CT angiography.** ABPI says how bad; CT angiography says where.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has a 2 month history of a painful punched-out ulcer on his left heel with calf pain on walking 50 metres. He smokes. The left foot is cool with absent pedal pulses. Investigations: left ABPI 0.52. He is referred to the vascular surgeons to confirm the arterial blockage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: CT angiography is the gold-standard investigation that confirms and assesses the arterial blockage before intervention.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
First-line ABPI is done; the gold standard confirms the blockage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CT angiography.

elim: Gives oxygenation and acid-base status, not limb anatomy.
For embolic sources in acute ischaemia, not chronic PAD.
For neurogenic claudication with normal pulses.
For neuropathy, not arterial disease.

steps.x: **B. CT angiography.** Gold standard for arterial ulcer/PAD = CT angiography.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a small arterial ulcer on his right lateral malleolus and calf claudication at 200 metres. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. His right ABPI is 0.7. He takes clopidogrel and atorvastatin, started last month. He has no rest pain. His BP is 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Smoking cessation and a supervised exercise programme
questions.e: First-line management is risk factor control: stop smoking and a supervised exercise programme, alongside antiplatelet and statin therapy.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Drugs are started; the missing first-line steps are lifestyle.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Smoking cessation and a supervised exercise programme.

elim: End-stage option for unsalvageable limbs.
Dangerous with an ABPI below 0.8; it worsens ischaemia.
For failure of conservative treatment or critical ischaemia.
No signs of infection.

steps.x: **E. Smoking cessation and a supervised exercise programme.** Arterial ulcer first-line: stop smoking, supervised exercise, antiplatelet, statin.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a punched-out ulcer on her left fourth toe. Her left ABPI is 0.65. She stopped smoking 3 months ago, attends a supervised exercise class and takes atorvastatin 80 mg. She has no history of bleeding. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm in sinus rhythm and BP 134/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which drug should be added?
questions.e: Antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel, or aspirin) is first-line in arterial ulcers from PAD to reduce atherosclerotic events; anticoagulation is not indicated in sinus rhythm.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Lifestyle and statin are done; the antiplatelet is missing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clopidogrel.

elim: Not part of PAD treatment and no indication here.
For fluid overload; may worsen limb perfusion.
Impairs wound healing; no inflammatory cause.
Anticoagulation is for AF or VTE; she is in sinus rhythm.

steps.x: **B. Clopidogrel.** PAD/arterial ulcer: clopidogrel (or aspirin) plus atorvastatin.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has an arterial ulcer on his right heel. He has stopped smoking and takes clopidogrel 75 mg. He has no other medication. Investigations: total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L (reference <5.0), LDL cholesterol 4.0 mmol/L (reference <3.0). His BP is 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to start?
questions.e: A high-intensity statin, atorvastatin, is first-line lipid-lowering therapy in PAD to slow atherosclerosis and reduce cardiovascular events.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Antiplatelet is on board; add lipid lowering.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Atorvastatin.

elim: Add-on if a statin is not tolerated or not enough.
For high triglycerides; not first-line for cardiovascular protection.
No outcome benefit; not used.
Not recommended for secondary prevention here.

steps.x: **A. Atorvastatin.** Arterial ulcer: atorvastatin for every patient.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a painful arterial ulcer on her left big toe. The pain is moderate and stops her enjoying walks. She has stopped smoking and takes clopidogrel and atorvastatin, and is awaiting vascular review. She has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73m². She has taken no analgesia yet.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial analgesia?
questions.e: Ulcer pain is treated with paracetamol first, escalating to opioid analgesia such as morphine only for severe pain.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Start at the bottom of the analgesic ladder.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Paracetamol.

elim: For neuropathic pain, not ischaemic ulcer pain.
NSAIDs carry renal and cardiovascular risk, especially with an eGFR of 38.
Reserved for severe pain after paracetamol.
For neuropathic pain.

steps.x: **D. Paracetamol.** Arterial ulcer pain: paracetamol, then opioids such as morphine.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a non-healing arterial ulcer on his right heel and rest pain. He stopped smoking and takes clopidogrel and atorvastatin. His right ABPI is 0.42. CT angiography shows a single 3 cm stenosis of the right superficial femoral artery with good vessels below. His BP is 136/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Definitive treatment is revascularisation; a short, focal stenosis is well suited to angioplasty.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Medical therapy has failed; there is a short lesion to open.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty.

elim: For unsalvageable limbs; this one can be revascularised.
Contraindicated with an ABPI below 0.8.
Debrides slough but does not restore blood flow.
Rarely used; not a revascularisation.

steps.x: **E. Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty.** Short focal stenosis = angioplasty; long occlusion = bypass.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has an arterial ulcer on her left lateral malleolus, rest pain and an ABPI of 0.35. She has stopped smoking and takes clopidogrel and atorvastatin. CT angiography shows a long occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery with a patent popliteal artery below the knee. She is otherwise fit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Definitive treatment is revascularisation; a long occlusion with a good distal target in a fit patient is treated by bypass surgery.
